newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bolger says suports NZ RSS scheme, will vote "yes".
newsitem.headline: Bolger says suports NZ RSS scheme, will vote "yes".

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Monday he supported a compulsory pension proposal, known as the Retirement Savings Scheme (RSS), put forward earlier in the day by Treasurer Winston Peters.
"I am supporting this scheme. It is a good design," he told reporters at a news conference.

In late February, when coalition MPs were being much more open than they are now about an agreement which will allow them a free vote in the RSS referendum, Bolger had said he would support a compulsory scheme only if it was a good one.
"I will personally vote 'yes'," he told reporters on Monday.
Despite his acceptance of the idea, Bolger said he did not anticipate "campaigning across the country" for RSS ahead of the September vote.
Asked in what way he thought the RSS concept had merits, he said it was better "than what we have now," adding "the status quo would have to be substantially amended to make it sustainable".

Critics led by the opposition Labour Party's finance spokesman Michael Cullen have noted that making the all-new RSS scheme acceptable to the earners who will have to start paying their own way relies on the state being able to phase in tax
cuts to compensate for the new contributions.
The phased tax cuts, in turn, depend on wider fiscal policy issues, according to today's RSS white paper.
Asked if there was any certainty for people that the tax cuts would remain in place once RSS was in place, Bolger said the only way to certainty was "to elect good government".
The prime minister was asked to asses the impact on the wider economy of linking the promised 1998 tax cut to the launch of RSS, which is the plan if the referendum result is a "yes".

It is stated government policy to proceed with the tax cut anyway, even if RSS is rejected, and economists say this would probably give the economy more of a boost, but Bolger would not be drawn on the relative merits of the two outcomes.
"There will be some debate on that impact...but there will be some reinvestment through the savings scheme (if it is voted in)," he replied.
